teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: Covered. ruleException (ruleException.ts:70), positionalRead's 'open the position before they catch up' (positionalRead.ts:273), and reviewSacrifice.sacrificeCompensation (reviewSacrifice.ts:44).

teachingMoves.move: States the plan as stages with checkpoints, and what happens if it fails
teachingMoves.example: Step one, keep their king from castling; step two, chase it toward f2; then attack. If they do manage to castle, your structure is sound and the game simply goes on.
teachingMoves.when: The start of the middlegame
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: Partial. nextPlans.deriveNextPlans (nextPlans.ts:161), speedRunReads' promise threads, and planMemory. The 'if it fails, you are still fine' risk check is MISSING.

teachingMoves.move: Transforms one kind of advantage into another (a slow positional edge into active play) and states the pros and cons of doing it

teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: Partial. positionTransformation.detectPositionTransformation (positionTransformation.ts:83) flags bad or missed trades. thinkAloud.lineAchieves notes a transformation into a pawn ending (thinkAloud.ts:86). A voluntary transformation with its pros and cons is MISSING.

teachingMoves.example: You are a piece up: put the rooks on the open files and let them trade. The bishop goes to f2, the safest square. / Pick the most economical win, not the flashiest.

'Trade to relieve pressure' is MISSING. moveInsight.materialPlan gives the opposite advice when down material (keep pieces on, moveInsight.ts:1012): right when lost, wrong when merely pressed.

summary:
Close second reading of public/data/voiced-teachings.json notes[3482..3925]: 444 notes from 19 videos. By phase: 160 opening, 194 middlegame, 90 endgame. The student is White in 166 notes and Black in 278. Method: I read every note against its board, checked 9 positions with chess.js, and compared the slice with the two coarse readers who covered it (docs/plans/swarm-inputs/digests/raw-teach.json readers 4 and 5, with 19 and 26 acts). Every computer mapping was grepped in src/services with tests excluded.

Result: 73 acts. 59 of them are missing from the coarse pass; the other 14 sharpen or correct a coarse act. Each is tagged [NEW], [SHARPENS] or [CORRECTS] in its `move` field. The F0c role it fills is in its `verb` field.

THE BIGGEST GAPS IN THIS SLICE, ranked by notes times teaching value:
1. MOVE ORDER FOR POSITIONAL REASONS: cover the square a pawn push gives up, bring out the guard before the piece whose move would drop a pawn, castle before opening the centre, develop before chasing. moveOrder.moveOrder (src/services/moveOrder.ts:65) speaks only when the wrong order loses material or mates (guards at :10-17, ORDER_COST_CP at :29), so none of these ever qualify.
2. A GOAL HELD ACROSS MOVES:
   - Keep the prize: kingSafety.castleRoute (src/services/kingSafety.ts:202) counts only the student's own pieces in the way (:207-213). It cannot see an enemy bishop covering f8; chess.js confirms the b4 bishop does exactly that at note 3832.
   - Revise the plan when their resource appears.
   - Change the route, not the plan.
   - The keystone move.
   planArc.stepArc (src/services/planArc.ts:236) records that a plan was given up (:329), never why.
3. OPENING TEACHING (F02), mostly MISSING:
   - why the opponent plays a move (a habit carried over from another opening) and the one-pawn antidote;
   - look-alike openings separated by one difference;
   - why a sideline exists and what neutralises it;
   - a method for when the opponent leaves book;
   - two practical rules for meeting a gambit;
   - a transposition you can decline.
   Partial support: openingIdentity.openingIdentityLine (src/services/openingIdentity.ts:85), openingBranches.branchesAt (src/services/openingBranches.ts:56), positionReadingService.structureTransfer (src/services/positionReadingService.ts:1047), which covers 3 structures only.
4. CALCULATION CRAFT:
   - why the check matters;
   - the reflex defence that drops a piece on the far side. refutedAlternativeCore.droppedJob (src/services/refutedAlternativeCore.ts:63) proves it, but it is never fed the opponent's defence;
   - a bait inside a capture;
   - checking whether a threat is real;
   - a sacrifice that isn't really one;
   - the guaranteed minimum of a sacrifice;
   - the opening's key motif re-checked at the end of every line;
   - settling the simplest question first.
5. STRUCTURE JUDGEMENTS: fix the target before attacking it, fix their pawns on your bishop's colour, blockade a pawn majority, doubled pawns as an asset, choosing between two pawn breaks.
6. THREADS ACROSS MOVES: voicing the objection to a counter-intuitive move before answering it, and naming the earlier quiet move whose point only shows now.

CORRECTIONS TO THE COARSE PASS:
(a) A live trapped-piece computer does exist: tacticsDetector.findTrappedPieces (src/services/tacticsDetector.ts:451, run inside detectTactics at :833) and reviewTeachingPoints.findTrappedPiece (src/services/reviewTeachingPoints.ts:789).
(b) The cheapest-defender half exists: moveInsight.pawnCanGuard (src/services/moveInsight.ts:889), spoken by positionAsk at :220.
(c) The queen standoff also maps to moveFundamentals 'queen-off-file' (src/services/moveFundamentals.ts:68), not only keepTension.
(d) A pin aimed at a defender is moveFundamentals 'attack-defender' (src/services/moveFundamentals.ts:53).

SIDE FINDINGS (flagged, not acted on):
- onlyMoveSequence.walkForcedSequence (src/services/onlyMoveSequence.ts:57) is the only computer that can prove a forced perpetual (terminus at :96-99), and it has zero production callers: built but unwired (G8.5).
- positionalRead.ts:394 trims the spoken list of weak-colour holes to two squares with cc.squares.slice(0, 2). That is a cap on a spoken computed fact (V14).
- reviewSacrifice.sacrificeCompensation (src/services/reviewSacrifice.ts:44) is called only from Review (reviewFullData.ts:915, coachFeatureService.ts:2750). Learn cannot say what a sacrifice bought (F2/S1).
- Source data:
  - 45 of the 444 notes speak in first person, and note 3634 names a content creator. danyaTeachingService.teachingBeatText (src/services/danyaTeachingService.ts:1605) joins the note fields verbatim, and I found no first-person filter on that path (V1/F0d).
  - Notes 3577, 3578 and 3659 carry a percentage, rating bands and a claim about players at a level (V8/F10).
  - Notes 3741-3742 sit one ply early: 3742's prose about a pawn going to the f-file is anchored on 18...dxe2.
  - Note 3687 calls the student's own knight on c6 'Black's' (V16).
- 35...axb1=N, an underpromotion at note 3515, goes untaught in the source: a rare fact the coach would need its own computer for.

rhythm:
Measured over the 444 notes:
- **Length:**
  - Average words: opening 25.2, middlegame 27.6, endgame 15.2.
  - 136 notes (31%) are under 12 words and 45 are 5 words or fewer.
  - 8 notes run over 80 words: #3944 170, #3978 570, #4012 180, #4209 85, #4213 152, #4288 154, #4340 87, #4344 86.
- **When he talks at length:** density follows how much the decision weighs, not the move number. The long lectures land where the opponent leaves book, where a tactic appears, or at the one strategic crossroads of the game. Quiet conversion drops to "you can simplify" or a bare capture.
- **Bare play-by-play:** one game, #4137–4188, is 50 of 52 notes under 12 words. That is description, not a rhythm to copy.
- **A thought often spans several moves.** 19 notes end mid-sentence and the idea finishes on the next one or two plies (#3936-37, #3962-65, #3969-71, #4006-09, #4213-17, #4278-83, #4342-43). Commentary runs continuously while the moves are played: a plan is stated across the plies that carry it out, and a setup move's purpose is paid off later (c6 at #3997 explained at #4001). Design note: the unit of teaching is the thought, not the ply. The composer must be able to open a thought on ply N and close it on N+1 or N+2.
- **Order inside a dense note:**
  1. the tempting or natural move;
  2. why it fails, concretely;
  3. the move;
  4. its reason;
  5. a one-line portable takeaway (72 notes carry one in `teaches`).

  The 570-word note #3978 runs the full F18 chain in order: risk assessed and dismissed with a resource, tension accepted, the glue move with its three jobs, what hangs and what doesn't, prophylaxis asked and answered, the piece kept for its duty, their aggressive-looking move reframed by its drawback, the line, the overload, the recap, then the king hunt as a method.
- **Questions:** 10 of the 11 question marks are rhetorical and answered at once. Thinking out loud in question form is not the F05 quiz.

teachingMoves.move: NEW — Your own quiet move unmasks a pin on your piece (the blocker sits BETWEEN your piece and your king)
teachingMoves.example: Careful with d3: it clears the line from their bishop on b4 through your knight to your king. From then on the knight on c3 is pinned, so when their knight lands on d5 yours can't take it.
teachingMoves.when: Opening and middlegame quiet pawn moves while an enemy bishop or rook already lines up through two of your pieces and your king

teachingMoves.move: NEW — Pieces have jobs that change over time: a job ends (the piece is freed), a job is handed to another piece, a piece is kept or held back because of its job
teachingMoves.example: The bishop on b4 has done its work (d5 isn't coming any more), so it is free to trade. After the recapture your queen takes over the knight's old job of guarding b2. Don't take on f3: this bishop's job is to keep that knight pinned. Don't rush the knight to the pretty square on d5, because right now it is the only thing guarding b2.
teachingMoves.when: Any move that changes who guards what, and before moving or trading a piece that holds a duty

teachingMoves.move: NEW — Heavy pieces make poor guards, attacking side: when a rook or queen is the only defender, harass it with pawns and minors until something drops
teachingMoves.example: Once the queens are off, their knight on d4 is guarded only by their rook, and a rook is a clumsy guard because any pawn can kick it with tempo. Tuck the bishop in, then push the f- and g-pawns at the rook until they have to give up the exchange.

teachingMoves.example: The knight to a4 looks natural, but b5 leaves it with no square, and that wins a piece. Their queen has run out of retreats: note it, and look for the pawn moves that cage it. Don't drop your knight into e4 here, because f3 traps it.

teachingMoves.move: NEW — Rescue your own stranded piece: bring the far-flung piece home in time, or free a trapped one with a tactic
teachingMoves.example: Your queen has wandered into the corner and could be cut off. Use the pin it creates: the bishop to h6 forces the queens off and gets it out. Before you press on, bring the queen back from the corner, ideally to a square where it still does a job.

teachingMoves.example: They haven't lost the right to castle, but they can't: your bishop on c5 covers g1. Every move they spend fixing that is a move you spend taking the centre, and if the king does get away it walks into a mess.

teachingMoves.example: Don't take on c3 just to double their pawns: here the doubled pawns don't hurt them and only tighten their grip on the centre. Your own doubled c-pawns aren't a liability either: they roll forward one after the other, and c5 later undoubles them.

So your choices are to ignore it and develop, or to hand the pawn back on your own terms (d3, forcing them to recapture instead of building a centre). As the gambiteer: f4 is offered for two things, a bigger centre with d4 and an open f-file for your rook once you castle.

summary:
Read every note in voiced-teachings.json notes[4370..4813]: 444 notes from 28 videos. Mapped 102 distinct teaching acts against src/services: 30 exist, 50 are partial (one of them is blocked by a gate), 22 are missing. The earlier census and the insight catalogue already cover the broad categories. This slice adds fine-grained acts that no computer produces.

WHAT THE COARSE READERS MISSED:
1. The 'a pinned piece is no guard' nugget, spoken in Learn or Review. Legal SEE counts it silently (positionReadingService.ts:212); only How-to-Think says it aloud (thinkingExchangeChain.ts:131).
2. What a pin is really aimed at: the job of the pinned piece.
3. 'Your move is good AND sets a trap for their natural reply', outside the gem library. trapAheadAt (gemCrushLines.ts:564) only covers curated gems for the side to move.
4. Trapped-piece detail: which piece covers each flight square, the threat to trap one move early, keeping the cage shut, and walking the king over to collect. findTrappedPiece (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:789) is present-tense only and generic (coachFeatureService.ts:3226).
5. Refuting THEIR in-between move, and praising the student's positional in-between move.
6. The wrong-recapture assumption.
7. Choosing mate over material, and the reverse.
8. The empty-check verdict (bluffDetector skips checks, bluffDetector.ts:33), and dismissing a back-rank alarm when they have no heavy piece.
9. Re-scanning the board after a flurry of exchanges.
10. King to b1 after castling long; pawn pushes that commit your castling side.
11. Preparing a recapture in advance.
12. A shiny one-move tactic versus the plan.
13. Move-order tempo arithmetic (keep the pawn home so the break costs one move), and opening trigger ideas.
14. Opening analogies, including reversed openings with an extra tempo.
15. Small edges accumulating.
16. Right idea, wrong piece.
17. The defender's accounting when the opponent's sacrifice overpays. sacrificeCompensation is Review-only and returns nothing on a losing sac (reviewSacrifice.ts:38/44).
18. Two minors against a rook. materialPlan covers only the rook side (moveInsight.ts:993).
19. Ranking the reasons for a move, raising the student's objection and answering it, and keeping brainstorm separate from forced lines.

GATE GAP: speedRunReads.anyMoveFine returns null once the eval passes 300cp (speedRunReads.ts:74). That is exactly where the reference coach says many moves win and you can pick any (4 notes).

DATA DEFECTS in this slice of shipped notes (spoken on S7 surfaces):
- 43/444 notes are in the first person (V1).
- 3 contain percentages (V8: #4501, #4509, #4741).
- 22 are cut mid-sentence at transcript boundaries.
- 1 credits a named person in the first person (F0d/V1: #4693).
- 2 promise an explanation later that never comes (#4526, #4724).
- 1 claim is verified false on its board (D10): vc-YzI6qI-33_U-16 (#4376) names an f4-pawn and a d4-bishop, but chess.js shows f4 empty and the bishop on e3. The note is anchored about five plies early.
rhythm:
Measured on all 444 notes: mean 28 words, median 23, p90 51, max 175.
- By phase: opening mean 26 (median 24). Middlegame mean 35 (p90 71); the long notes are decision points (which capture, whether to sacrifice, which side to castle), weighing 2-3 candidates with the opponent's replies in 60-175 words. Endgame mean 17.5; these are technique verdicts (only square, up a whole knight, rook behind the pawn).
- Opponent's moves get as many words as the student's (28.1 vs 28.0). What their move does, costs or threatens is narrated just as fully.
- Bare description: 48/444 (11%) are one clause with no reason (9 words or fewer, no connective). 20 of them come from one distilled game (yt:Zko_JUK06vM: 51 notes averaging 6 words), so this is distillation variance, not his teaching. Elsewhere even routine moves carry a purpose clause (preparing b4, tucking the king away).
- Ply coverage: notes exist on 64% of plies inside each game's span (444 of 692). The distillation drops plies, so a gap here is not evidence that he was silent.
- Shape of a long note: what the move does, then the tempting alternative and its concrete refutation, then the line with their replies in words, then the count or verdict, then the principle or habit.
- Openings front-load identity in moves 1-6: name, philosophy, main line vs sideline, the slip typical at the level. Middlegames lead with the threat or plan and weigh candidates. Endgames lead with the technique and stop.
- About 11 rhetorical question-then-answer pairs model the student's own thinking.

teachingMoves.move: Name the opening as it appears and say what the whole opening is trying to do
teachingMoves.example: After the knight to f6 and the pawn to d6, this is the give-them-the-centre defence for real: you let them build a big centre now and plan to hit it from the side later; the whole game becomes whether you crack it before they use it.
teachingMoves.when: moves 1-6, the move that defines or changes the opening
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL: naming via openingDetectionService.detectOpening (openingDetectionService.ts:166) and openingAnnouncement (openingAnnouncement.ts:54); philosophy via openingIdentity.openingIdentityLine (openingIdentity.ts:85: provokes/aims/gambit/sharp/famous). The game's strategic question (who wins the race for the centre) is not computed.

teachingMoves.move: Grade the opponent's opening choice against theory and name the main move it is not
teachingMoves.example: Their queen to d2 is a lesser sideline; the usual move is the bishop to c4. Their bishop to d3 shows they've left book, and it doesn't do the job the c4-square would.
teachingMoves.when: opponent's move that leaves the main line
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL: bookDeparture (bookDeparture.ts:49), theoryDeparture.findTheoryDeparture (theoryDeparture.ts:73), strongChoice (strongChoice.ts:16), refutedAlternative (refutedAlternative.ts:81). Missing: what the main move does that theirs does not; moveContrast.contrastMoves (moveContrast.ts:64) only compares which pieces each move leaves undefended.

teachingMoves.move: NEW: move-order tempo arithmetic: keep a pawn at home so its break costs one move, and avoid the order that lets them transpose
teachingMoves.example: Castle but leave the d-pawn at home: from d7 it reaches d5 in one move later, while d6 now would let them switch to the sharper f3 set-up and cost you a tempo when you break.
teachingMoves.when: opening, choosing which move comes first
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL: speedRunReads.flexibleFirst (speedRunReads.ts:549) says piece first, pawn later. MISSING: the double-step tempo count for a delayed break, and the transposition-avoidance reason (the only double-step read is endgamePawnReads.ts:157, for pawn endings).

teachingMoves.move: Name the transposition as the point of the move
teachingMoves.example: Hitting their centre pawn with the knight instead of taking the gambit pawn forces a calm c3-Sicilian structure, with far less theory than the accepted gambit.
teachingMoves.when: opening, the move that changes which opening it is
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL: detectOpening (openingDetectionService.ts:166) can see the new name; no service turns 'this transposes into X, and that is why' into teaching.

teachingMoves.move: Opening analogy: this is opening X with one difference, and the difference changes the plan
teachingMoves.example: It's the fianchetto set-up without their c-pawn on c4, so the game turns tactical. In the plain London you'd answer ...c5 with c3, but your knight is on c3, so take on c5 instead. Against 1.e3 you are playing a French with an extra move.
teachingMoves.when: opening, the structure matches a sibling opening
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING: positionReadingService.namedPawnStructure (positionReadingService.ts:1060) names a structure but never compares it with a sibling opening; no service detects a reversed opening with an extra tempo.

teachingMoves.move: Practical gambit handling: decline cleanly, and say why
teachingMoves.example: Decline the pawn: taking it is playable but you must know a lot to survive, which is the fight they want. The best decline develops and hits their centre at the same time.
teachingMoves.when: facing a gambit offer
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL: openingIdentity's gambit fact (how long the material imbalance lasts, openingIdentity.ts:124). The accept/decline advice is repertoire guidance with no computer.

teachingMoves.move: Mark the slip that players at your level typically make here
teachingMoves.example: The bishop check on f2 is the standard error at this level; taking on f6 here is a frequent blunder because people expect the bishop to take back.
teachingMoves.when: known slip positions, usually the opponent's natural move
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL: gems mined at rating bands, gemCrushLines.trapAheadAt / gemMoveSignal (gemCrushLines.ts:564/582); safetyHabits.autopilotGuard (safetyHabits.ts:42) uses the popular move at the student's level. Outside the gem library, nothing says 'this is the usual mistake here'.

rhythm:
Measured on the 444 notes:
- Length: median 25 words a ply, mean 29, p90 57, max 143. Opening: median 26, mean 29. Middlegame: median 27, mean 31. Endgame: median 20, mean 24. Endgame talk is short and rule-like (active king, pawn colour, fortress, push the majority).
- Coverage: in the full-game streams he speaks on 90-100% of plies. Overall coverage within each video's span is 68%, because distilled lesson videos keep only key moments. A played game is effectively never silent.
- Their move vs yours: he says MORE on the OPPONENT's move (mean 31, p90 67) than on the student's (mean 28, p90 47). The thinking happens when they move: what it changed, what it wants, what to do about it. The student's own move often gets a short confirmation.
- Bare dictations: 8% of notes are 6 words or fewer. They come in runs through book or forced sequences (a gambit's moves dictated one by one), followed by a burst.
- Thoughts span plies: 22% of notes start mid-sentence and 15% end open. One thought regularly runs across two or three plies, so the narration is a stream, not one card per move.
- Where the bursts land: the longest notes (90-143 words) come at the first out-of-book decision (a survey of options with a reason each), at a gambit's compensation summary, and at a tactical crux with branching lines.
- Order inside a burst: what their move does or wants → what you would like and what is in the way → the tempting or natural option and why it fails → the chosen move with its line and their reply → the rule or habit, usually last. This matches F18.
- Language mix: 43% carry an explicit because/so/but link, 9% an if-then branch, 10% a question, 86% name a square, 61% address 'you', and 16% are first person (to be converted). Almost none use numbers; one 'ninety-five percent' frequency claim was the lone hit.

summary:
Close second reading of public/data/voiced-teachings.json notes[5258..5701]: 444 notes from 31 videos (240 opening, 178 middlegame, 26 endgame; 360 with the student as White). I read every note, then checked each act against all 642 acts in docs/plans/swarm-inputs/digests/teach.md. Reader 6 covered this slice coarsely, inside a 1,500-note pass. Every code citation below was opened and checked at the cited line.

WHAT THE COARSE READERS MISSED. 21 acts in this slice have no counterpart in the coarse digest; they are listed first and marked NEW. Most are conditions and geometry, not whole new topics:
- Not every check is good.
- A committed pawn can no longer block a check.
- Make their KING do the recapturing.
- A hole guarded only by a piece is still a hole.
- Don't capture with the piece that holds your net.
- Short-run asset, long-run liability.
- The price of opening a line, and whether the king can just leave.
- Lure their piece onto a square you can kick with tempo.
- Trade off their only developed piece.
- A bishop behind your own pawn is loaded.
- Keep their piece where it clogs their own system.
- Don't park a piece on your own open file.
- Don't cage your own piece with a pawn move.
- Keep the pawn that can still kick their piece.
- Keep a standing watch on their one break.
- Allow their break when they can't support it.
- Name the defender's method.
- Mate threat plus material threat in one move.
- Deny castling through the transit square.
- Know the pawn that stalls a storm.
- Trust the attacker count (only when the engine agrees).

Five refinements follow. They sharpen acts the coarse readers had, including the self-answered question, which is NOT an F05 question.

The canonical example for questions.md item 7 sits in this slice, at #5408-5414. I checked it with chess.js: after the knight takes on e5 with check, the pinning bishop on g4 is attacked by the knight and the queen and defended once. By material count that sequence nets pawns, not a piece. So under F04 it is a pattern taught with its conditions, not a trap, and David's first gem may need the engine to clear F04's piece bar.

- 51 skip one, 22 skip two or more.
- Own move median 20 words vs 15 on the opponent's move. He says more as his own move is played, and thinks while their move is on the board.
- 44% of notes over 9 words carry an explicit link (because, so, but, instead, the point, rather than, if).
- 13 notes (3%) end mid-thought and finish on the next ply.

Long monologues: only 5 notes reach 90+ words (#5322, #5327 at about 820, #5332, #5467, #5545). All sit at plies 6-20. They lay out a whole plan or a whole lesson at one decision point.

Order inside a long note (#5286, #5322, #5408, #5420, #5545):
1. What their move did or threatens.
2. What the student is probably thinking (a worry or a tempting move).
3. Why that falls short, with a short line.
4. The move and its one deciding reason.
5. The line played out with their reply.
6. A habit or tip to close.

The opening is explained move by move with the theory status. Middlegame decision points get the deliberation. Forced replies get 3-8 words. Only 3% of notes contain a question mark, and every one is answered in the same breath.

teachingMoves.move: NEW - Judges a check by the opponent's best answer: a check is good only if the block or king move doesn't hand something back; chooses between two checks by what each wins
teachingMoves.example: When you're already a piece up, the bishop check on b5 looks like free development. But their c-pawn blocks it while hitting the bishop, and the tactic that follows only swaps two of your minor pieces for a rook and two pawns, so you'd hand material back for nothing. Elsewhere: of two queen checks, pick the one that collects a pawn on the way.
teachingMoves.when: Converting a won position; any check that 'develops with tempo'; choosing between checks
teachingMoves.frequency: 4 notes (#5286 refuted check; #5291, #5327, #5545 choosing the right check). 0 hits for 'not every check' in the coarse digest.
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. playCommentary.ts:497 buildRejectedTempting refutes a tempting capture or check from the multipv lines (at least 1.5 pawns worse). Two problems: playCommentary.ts:533 skips it whenever the student still stands 2+ pawns up after the check, which is #5286's exact case; and CoachTeachPage.tsx:220 caps the beat at 2 per game (applied at CoachTeachPage.tsx:9852), a count cap that V14 forbids. Choosing between two checks: MISSING.

teachingMoves.move: NEW - Notices that a pawn already committed can no longer block a future check, so that check becomes the target of your next moves
teachingMoves.example: Their c-pawn has already gone to c5, so a later bishop check on b5 can't be met by c6. With their queen and king lined up on the e-file, your quiet moves are building toward exactly that check.
teachingMoves.when: When the opponent pushes the pawn that used to be their interposing pawn
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. checkMethod.ts:32 reads only the student's own answers when they are already in check (answer kinds at checkMethod.ts:46). latentDanger.ts:87 reads alignments against the student's own king and queen. Nothing counts the opponent's future interpositions.

teachingMoves.move: NEW - Makes THEIR king do the recapturing: a queen trade that strips castling and leaves the king badly placed even with queens off
teachingMoves.example: Take on e4. After the pawn trade you swap queens with a capture on d1, their king has to take back, and it sits on d1 for the rest of the game: no castling, and in its own pieces' way.
teachingMoves.when: Early opening exchanges where the queens can come off on the king's file
teachingMoves.frequency: 3 notes, one idea (#5319-5321); chess.js-verified (White's castling rights are gone after the king recaptures).
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL, blocked by a gate. theirMoveCost.ts:117-130 names 'castling given up', but only while queens are on (theirMoveCost.ts:120-121, reasoned at :118-119), so this exact case is silenced by design. recaptureChoice.ts:91 flags 'would give up castling' only for the student's own king. The gate should key on phase (an early queenless middlegame with every minor piece on is not an ending), not on whether queens are on.

teachingMoves.move: NEW - Answers the objection 'but they cover that square': a hole guarded only by a PIECE is still a hole; occupying it forces the guard to trade itself, and trades help the side that is ahead
teachingMoves.example: Yes, their dark bishop watches d6. That doesn't fix the hole. Put the knight there anyway, and if the bishop takes it that's one more trade, which is what you want when you're a queen up. That's also why you give up the bishop and keep the knight.
teachingMoves.when: When the student hesitates over an outpost an enemy piece watches; trades near a hole
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. outpost.ts:22 noPawnCanChallenge and outpost.ts:39 isOutpost already count only PAWN guards, so the square is computed as a hole. speedRunReads.ts:337 rightPieceForHole prefers the knight. tradeJudgement.ts:74 says trades favour the side ahead. MISSING: the joined sentence (a piece guard can be traded off, a pawn guard can't).

teachingMoves.move: NEW - Before grabbing, checks whether the capturing unit is part of your net: taking with it lets the trapped piece escape
teachingMoves.example: Their knight jumps to g5 and hits your queen. Taking it with the f-pawn feels natural, but that pawn is what covers e5, the trapped queen's only exit. Step your queen back to e2 instead, and their queen stays caged.

The middlegame deliberation (deliberation.ts:144) has shortfall kinds drops-material, trades-queens, clearly-worse and less-precise (deliberation.ts:66), and filters out alternatives with no material proof (deliberation.ts:278). So the reason never speaks there. Wire droppedJob into deliberation.

teachingMoves.example: A queen up, shed a pawn to open the centre, since in a closed position the queen has nothing to do. But giving a knight to rip open the e-file buys nothing: their king castles to the other wing, and the open file has no one left to attack.

teachingMoves.move: NEW - A bishop aimed behind your own advanced pawn is loaded: when the pawn moves, the line opens all at once

teachingMoves.move: NEW - Doesn't park a piece on your own open file
teachingMoves.example: The bishop to f4 looks active, but it plugs the f-file your rook is using. Push e5 instead: it kicks their knight off f6, and after the exchange the file stays open for the rook and queen to come at the king.

teachingMoves.example: You might be nervous about their knight on e5, but what is it actually attacking? Nothing; you'll trade it later. Or you might think their bishop fixes the hole, but it doesn't (see the piece-guarded hole above).

teachingMoves.move: REFINEMENT - Asks itself a question and answers it in the same breath, modelling the student's inner voice; this is thinking out loud (F0/F18), not an F05 question

teachingMoves.example: Giving up the fianchettoed bishop looks reckless, but your knight covers the sensitive squares, so their dark-square play goes nowhere. Likewise, make luft with g6 rather than h6: their bishop on d3 still covers h7, and they have no dark-squared bishop to use the holes g6 leaves.

teachingMoves.example: After the bishop pins your knight from g4, the bishop sacrifice on f7 lets that knight capture on e5 WITH CHECK. The pin is gone, and their bishop is now hit twice and guarded once. The only defence was a knight move to d7 covering e5.

teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. moveInsight.ts:701 escapeSquareFirst, tacticsDetector.ts:630 findRemovableGuards (guards of pieces, not of mating squares), reviewForcedSequence.ts:107 (deflection off the mating square, Review only).

teachingMoves.move: Wing-attack principles: castle opposite, don't storm where your own king lives, close the centre first, secure the spearhead before the break, finish development mid-attack
teachingMoves.example: Castle long so your kingside pawns are free to go. Close the centre with d5 so nothing distracts you. Support the g4 pawn with f3 before forcing the h-file open. Bring the last piece into the attack.
teachingMoves.when: Before and during pawn storms
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. kingAttack.ts:71, splitPosition.ts:14, reviewTeachingPoints.ts:557 describeNotableMove (Review only).

teachingMoves.move: When winning: take what's hanging, several moves win, don't give material back unless it removes their only active piece, don't get fancy
teachingMoves.example: There are a few ways to finish; the simplest is to take the loose pawn. A piece up, it's fine to return a pawn if that trades off their only developed minor and keeps your king safe.
teachingMoves.when: Decisive advantage
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: COMPUTED/PARTIAL. speedRunReads.ts:68 anyMoveFine, conversionMethod.ts:44 readConversion, safetyHabits.ts:54 keepPressing. Giving material back is MISSING (as reader 6 found).

teachingMoves.move: Their move's cost, and what they should have played (the antidote or improvement), including crediting a good defensive resource
teachingMoves.example: Their queen check from e6 blocks their own bishop and walks into your pieces. They had to know the knight move to d7 that covers e5. Their knight to g5 was a good try, credit to them.
teachingMoves.when: Opponent slips and opponent resources
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: COMPUTED/PARTIAL. theirMoveCost.ts:60, positionReadingService.ts:527-531 (knight on the rim), backwardLook.ts:98, inaccuracyCall.ts:194. Crediting their resource is MISSING.

teachingMoves.move: Rule and its exception; threat stronger than execution; patience and accumulation; callback to an earlier move's point
teachingMoves.example: A knight on the rim is fine as a stopover on its way to c4. Don't cash in yet; keeping them tied to the weak pawn hurts more. That's why the bishop went to f5 earlier: now it and the knight gang up on c2.
teachingMoves.when: Quiet manoeuvring and payoff moments
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. ruleException.ts:70 (three rules only), speedRunReads.ts:144 threatStronger, planArc.ts:236 stepArc. Accumulation is MISSING.

teachingMoves.move: Analogy and transfer: the same idea from another opening, or 'you already know this one'
teachingMoves.example: c6 against this gambit is the Caro-Kann idea: prepare d5. Against an early a6 Scandinavian you play exactly as against the normal one, developing the knight to c3 with tempo.
teachingMoves.when: A familiar idea in a new setting
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. motifLedger.ts:31 transferClause, structureSignature.ts:65 and :165 (used to pick notes, never spoken as an analogy).

teachingMoves.move: A piece standing in front of its own pawn takes that pawn's jobs away, most sharply when the blocked pawn was the only one that could ever support a neighbour: the neighbour becomes an isolated pawn in all but name
teachingMoves.example: After the early pawn swaps on d5, their knight comes to c3, right in front of the c2-pawn. No pawn can now ever come to c3 to back up d4, so while the knight stands there d4 is as weak as an isolated pawn. The sturdier set-up was the bishop to d3 and then c3, a pawn guarding a pawn.
teachingMoves.when: A developing move (theirs or the student's) lands directly in front of an own pawn in the opening: c3 in front of c2, f3 in front of f2, a bishop in front of the g-pawn
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (5748, 84 words, the longest opening note in the slice); the same family elsewhere in the corpus: a knight blocking the f-pawn a plan needs (727), a knight on c3 blocking the c-pawn's lever (2974), a bishop on g5 slowing its own side's g-pawn storm (6850)
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. boardStructure.ts:127-134 calls a pawn isolated only when no own pawn stands on an adjacent file, so d4 with c2 behind the knight never counts; describeConcessions reports only a true new isolani (reviewTeachingPoints.ts:745-746); theirMoveCost's kinds are hole / bishop-shut / castling / structure and its hole and bishop checks run only for pawn moves (theirMoveCost.ts:23, :73, :95); concessionBeat's DrawbackKind has no blocked-pawn kind (concessionBeat.ts:31-36). Buildable on findWeakPawns (positionReadingService.ts:1176): an adjacent-file pawn whose advance square holds its own piece gives no support.

teachingMoves.move: Hold a resource in reserve until the opponent's commitment makes it bite, and say the condition: a pin, a queen sortie, a lever or a pawn freeze is often worth a move only after one specific enemy move
teachingMoves.example: Don't give the check on b4 yet. That bishop earns its move once their knight stands on c3, because then taking it doubles their pawns; with only e3 played they simply block on d2 and you have spent a move for nothing. In the same spirit, the a4 freeze against their b-pawn can wait until that advance is really coming; bring a rook over first.
teachingMoves.when: Opening moves where a known motif's target has not committed yet; quiet middlegames where the opponent's break is still a move or two away
teachingMoves.frequency: 2 in slice (5905, 5954); the same held-back-until-they-commit shape about 10 times across the corpus (905 queen sortie strong only after their c3, 1157, 2974, 3649, 5545, 6586). Earlier readers caught only its capture form (the threat is stronger than its execution), the premature fork trick, and freezing a wing pawn after it advances
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING as a general read. speedRunReads.threatStronger keeps only a CAPTURE hanging (speedRunReads.ts:144); moveIntent says what a played move prevents or prepares, never 'this works once they play X' (moveIntent.ts:124); pinGeometry.pinBites prices a pin only in material (pinGeometry.ts:178-187), so the structural payoff that makes Bb4 worth a move (the capture that doubles their pawns) is never computed, although tradeQuality.recaptureDamage already classifies doubled / isolated / king-cover for a recapture (tradeQuality.ts:71).

teachingMoves.move: A conditional verdict on the move itself: this capture or commitment is sound only if one specific follow-up comes next, said before the follow-up is played
teachingMoves.example: Their capture on e4 is not a mistake, but it binds them to one answer: the ...e5 strike against your two centre pawns. The coach says so on the capture, then credits them when the strike arrives.
teachingMoves.when: Opening captures and commitments whose soundness hinges on the very next move
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (6035; the follow-up lands two plies later, 6037)
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. criticalMoment.readCriticalMoment counts how many moves hold on the CURRENT board (criticalMoment.ts:164); run on the board after their capture it would show that only one reply keeps the balance, but no lane speaks the forward 'fine only if' verdict on the capture itself.

teachingMoves.move: Refute a pawn grab by what it does to your king, not by material: the capture lets them trade queens on the d-file and your king has to take back, losing castling
teachingMoves.example: Taking on e5 is still wrong here. There is no check to fear any more, but the capture lets them swap queens on d1, your king must recapture, and it is stuck in the centre for the rest of the game. Develop instead.
teachingMoves.when: Early central captures that open the d-file while both queens face each other on it
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (6039); not in the coarse digest
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. recaptureChoice says 'would give up castling' only when the recapturing piece is itself the king (recaptureChoice.ts:91); speedRunReads.forceConcession names lost castling only for the OPPONENT after the student's forcing move (speedRunReads.ts:524); refutedAlternativeCore.renderRefutedAlternative refutes by a tactic concept, a proven material line, a dropped job or a cost in words (refutedAlternativeCore.ts:98-148), with no castling-loss reason.

teachingMoves.move: Prepare the recapture before the capture comes: put a piece where it can take back, so their capture cannot damage your pawn structure
teachingMoves.example: Their bishop pins your knight on c6 and wants to double your c-pawns. The queen to b6 answers that in advance: if the bishop takes on c6, the queen takes back and your pawns stay whole.
teachingMoves.when: The opponent threatens a capture whose pawn recapture would double or isolate your pawns
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. recaptureChoice runs only after a capture has happened (recaptureChoice.ts:103); moveIntent.whatItDoes describes what a move prepares only as castling, hitting a target or taking a file (moveIntent.ts:429-460); tradeQuality.recaptureDamage knows a pawn recapture would double or isolate (tradeQuality.ts:71) but nothing asks it before the capture.

teachingMoves.move: Recapture reasons the coach gives that the recapture computer cannot say: take back with the piece that keeps your options open; trade with check first and let them show how they take back; recapture with the pawn so a square opens for your other piece
teachingMoves.example: Take back on d4 with the pawn: the knight would commit too early, while after the pawn you can still choose between grabbing on e4 and a quiet rook move. Later, swap rooks on e1 with check first and see which piece they take back with. And if your knight is ever exchanged on e4, recapture with the d-pawn so d5 is free for the other knight.
teachingMoves.when: Every exchange with more than one recapture, and exchanges where giving check first forces their choice
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. readRecapture's reasons are: opens a file for the rook, toward the centre, doubles, isolates, frees the bishop, the knight lands centrally, loses the piece, the queen gets hit with tempo, gives up castling (recaptureChoice.ts:60-92). Missing: keeps options open, keeps contact with a target pawn, vacates a square for another piece. speedRunReads.flexibleFirst is the only keep-your-options read and it returns null on any capture (speedRunReads.ts:549-553).

teachingMoves.move: A threat to wreck the structure counts as a threat: a move that unmasks a capture which would double the pawns in front of their king
teachingMoves.example: Pushing the c-pawn opens your b7-bishop's diagonal, and now it threatens to take on f3; if the g-pawn takes back, the pawns in front of their castled king are wrecked.
teachingMoves.when: Moves that unmask a bishop or rook onto a knight guarded by a pawn next to the enemy king
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (5777); the digest has it only inside a several-jobs example
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. Threats are only mate / fork / capture (groundedAnswer.ts:6865); moveIntent.whatItDoes counts a hit only on a loose or higher-value target (moveIntent.ts:443-450), so a bishop eyeing a guarded knight of equal value gives no reason; tradeQuality.recaptureDamage already returns doubled / isolated / king-cover for a recapture (tradeQuality.ts:71) and is never asked about a threatened one.

teachingMoves.move: Whose key pawn advance lands first decides the opening: when one side never finds time for its thematic push, the other side plays it instead and takes the space
teachingMoves.example: This reversed King's Indian is dangerous for them precisely because they never get time for ...e5, so you are the one who plants a pawn on e5, and the space and the kingside attack are yours.
teachingMoves.when: Mirror or reversed structures where both sides aim at the same central advance
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (5850); the no-time-for shape about 3 times in the corpus (1232, 3263, 5850)
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. planRace races only two passed pawns or one shared open file (planRace.ts:26-40, detectPlanRace :180); tempoCount counts their repeated moves (tempoCount.ts:32); moveIntent's PREVENTS can say a move stops their push (moveIntent.ts:124) but not whose key advance arrives first.

teachingMoves.move: Name the shelter on a line: a king can hide behind a piece standing on the attacking line, even the attacker's OWN piece; the cure is to move that shield off the line with a threat so the line opens with tempo
teachingMoves.example: After the bishop takes on f7 with check, the king steps to f8 and hides behind your own bishop. Your rook on f1 looks up a file blocked by your knight on f3 and your bishop on f7, so moving the knight uncovers nothing yet. First take the bishop off the f-file with a move that demands an answer (it steps to e6 and offers itself again); then the knight's move uncovers the rook against the king.
teachingMoves.when: Right after a sacrifice or check when the defending king steps behind the attacker's piece; also when your queen recaptures behind your own pawn so the pawn shields it
teachingMoves.verb: RECOGNIZE (named defensive pattern) / PLAN (remove the obstacle)
teachingMoves.frequency: 2 in slice (6045-6046); the same shelter image once more for a queen behind its own pawn (6181)
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. findDiscoveredAttacks reads only the first two pieces on a ray and drops it when the second is your own (tacticsDetector.ts:571, :583-585), so a rook behind two of its own pieces in front of the king is invisible; latentDanger.detectLatentDanger is the student-side mirror, with at most one own shield in front of a king or queen (latentDanger.ts:87, :113-119). Nothing names the king sheltering behind the attacker's piece or proposes moving that shield with a threat; the tempo test at tacticsDetector.ts:607-610 is the reusable part.

teachingMoves.move: The in-between move instead of the automatic recapture (caught by earlier readers), listed here because the record half is missing
teachingMoves.example: Their bishop takes on e4, correctly, and you don't take back on reflex: push the d-pawn to d6 first, forking queen and minor piece while their bishop still hangs. In another game, after their bishop takes on c3, the pawn takes on c6 instead and they must lose the queen or the bishop.
teachingMoves.when: Inside exchanges, whenever the recapture looks automatic
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: TEACH half computed: thinkAloud.notYet (thinkAloud.ts:145, called :273) and moveInsight.autopilotRecapture (moveInsight.ts:642, whose only production caller is the puzzle wrong-try line, PuzzleBoard.tsx:652). RECORD half MISSING (F4/F5): positionPosed's comment lists the autopilot recapture (moveInsight.ts:731-732) but its body never poses it (moveInsight.ts:743-761); 'zwischenzug' is a TacticType (types/index.ts:1714) with no live detector (tacticVocabulary.ts:58-64), so detectTacticType files a missed in-between move from a real game under another motif or 'tactical_sequence' (missedTacticService.ts:770-808). The same holds for 'deflection' and 'interference' (types/index.ts:1709, :1713).

teachingMoves.move: Maintenance trade: not every exchange wins something; when your pawn is attacked and cannot be held, trading it off is just keeping the balance, and the coach says that
teachingMoves.example: Your e5-pawn is attacked and can't be kept, so take on d4. The trade wins nothing; it simply stops you losing a pawn, and now you get on with development.
teachingMoves.when: Central tension where your pawn is attacked more often than it can be defended
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. tradeJudgement returns null on any pawn capture (tradeJudgement.ts:47) and its reasons are their-best / gave-best / ahead / behind / bad-bishop / attacker-gone (tradeJudgement.ts:25); speedRunReads.keepTension goes silent when the capture IS the engine's move (speedRunReads.ts:57), so nothing explains why releasing the tension is right here. The fact is one exchange count away (legalSeeGainFor, positionReadingService.ts:212).

teachingMoves.move: A trade whose real point is the recapture: the piece that takes back abandons a defensive duty
teachingMoves.example: Offer the queen trade on d4 even though trading feels passive: when their rook takes back, it leaves the back rank, and from then on their knight on e5 cannot move without allowing mate on the back rank. The next moves pile on that frozen knight.
teachingMoves.when: Exchange offers where the recapturing piece is the only guard of something (the back rank, a piece)
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (6010), built on for four more plies (6011-6014)
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. tradeJudgement and tradeQuality.readTrade judge the pieces traded (tradeJudgement.ts:25; tradeQuality.ts:124), not what the recapturing piece leaves; findRemovableGuards is capture-the-guard (tacticsDetector.ts:630); weakenedBy tracks pieces losing guards, not an empty back rank (moveInsight.ts:523); 'deflection' has no live detector (tacticVocabulary.ts:58-64).

teachingMoves.move: Diagnose why their position is stuck: one weak pawn ties down the piece that must develop, so every developing move costs material except one; take that one away and they have nothing
teachingMoves.example: Their dark bishop can only come out with tempo on g5; anywhere else and their b2-pawn drops. Step your queen off that bishop's line in advance and they are left without a useful move: the whole position hangs on b2.
teachingMoves.when: The opponent's undeveloped minor is the only guard of an attacked pawn
teachingMoves.frequency: 3 in slice (5890, 5895, 5896); 'they are paralysed / stuck' verdicts about 12 times across the corpus
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. pieceOptions.dutiesOf finds the duty, pawns included (pieceOptions.ts:63), and computePieceOptions refutes each square (pieceOptions.ts:126), but its only caller is the chat question path (coach/coachService.ts:1507). findOverloadedPieces skips any target worth under 3 (tacticsDetector.ts:699), so 'their bishop alone guards b2' never reads as a tie; speedRunReads.takeTheSting defuses a threat to YOUR piece (speedRunReads.ts:400), not their only tempo move.

teachingMoves.move: Duty parity: before treating a tied defender as a cost, look at what the attacker is tied to; if their attacking piece is just as bound to the attack, it is a fair trade of duties
teachingMoves.example: If their queen comes after your b-pawn, guard it with a rook. Yes, the rook is now stuck on defence, but their queen is just as stuck on the attack, and neither piece does anything else.
teachingMoves.when: An enemy heavy piece probes a pawn and the cheapest adequate guard is a rook
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. moveInsight.heavyTiedDown flags only your own heavy piece as a sole guard, as a cost (moveInsight.ts:1022); pieceOptions.dutiesOf lists a defender's duties (pieceOptions.ts:63); nothing reads what the attacking piece is tied to.

teachingMoves.move: Before kicking a piece with a pawn, check where it lands: a careless kick hands it a better square. Cover its landing square first, then chase it toward the rim
teachingMoves.example: Pushing a pawn at their knight right away would only send it to a fine new square in your camp. Close that square with another pawn first, then chase the knight into the corner with the rook-pawn, and only then advance the f-pawn: one pawn shuts the door, the other does the pushing.
teachingMoves.when: An enemy knight sits well placed in front of your pawns and you want to drive it back
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (5955); its sibling, taking away the retreat square first (5950), an earlier reader logged as missing
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. moveInsight.noRetreat is about your own piece facing a pawn push (moveInsight.ts:957); findTrappedPieces needs the piece already attacked (tacticsDetector.ts:468-472); no read scores a pawn kick by the kicked piece's best landing square (outpost.isOutpost on the board after the kick would answer it, outpost.ts:39).

teachingMoves.move: The semi-outpost: a central square an enemy pawn could challenge only one day and at some cost; worth routing a knight to instead of opening the centre
teachingMoves.example: Rather than breaking in the centre, which would only open lines for them, send the knight to d5. It is not a true outpost, since their e-pawn could one day come to e4, but for now it is a fine central post.
teachingMoves.when: Closed or semi-closed centres with no true outpost available
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. outpost.isOutpost is binary: any enemy pawn that can ever reach an attacking square disqualifies the square (outpost.ts:22-39); findPieceQuality praises only a pawn-supported knight on a true outpost (positionReadingService.ts:526-535).

teachingMoves.move: A pawn break whose purpose is to get rid of YOUR weak pawn: trading off the backward pawn removes the target the game was revolving around
teachingMoves.example: Once their knight drops back, push d5: it is the direct way to get rid of your weak d6-pawn, and the open centre then favours your better bishop.
teachingMoves.when: You carry a backward or isolated pawn and an advance can trade it off safely
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (5882, after 5880 weighed that weakness against four strengths)
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING as a reason. findPawnBreaks admits a break by pawn contact and a safe landing (positionReadingService.ts:400, :425-435) and never says what the break fixes; findWeakPawns lists backward pawns (positionReadingService.ts:1176) but no read compares them before and after the break.

teachingMoves.move: Name the square that will become weak once the pawn guarding it is traded away, before the exchange happens
teachingMoves.example: Take on g6 with the h-pawn: besides opening the h-file, it is aimed at e6, which loses its pawn guard once their f7-pawn is drawn away to recapture.
teachingMoves.when: Pawn exchanges near the enemy king or in the centre that will remove a pawn guard
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING as a forward read. theirMoveCost's hole and moveInsight.holeAccess read only the hole a move just made (theirMoveCost.ts:72-91; moveInsight.ts:1102); weakenedBy tracks pieces, not squares (moveInsight.ts:523). Running outpost.noPawnCanChallenge on the end of the engine's exchange line would give it (outpost.ts:22).

teachingMoves.move: Restriction as an asset: a piece that takes away the enemy rooks' entry squares is worth keeping and defending, and the coach names that as the bonus of the move
teachingMoves.example: Taking on c2 wins a pawn, and the bishop there also keeps their rooks off b1 and d1. A piece that good is worth protecting rather than trading.
teachingMoves.when: A minor piece lands deep in the enemy camp on squares their rooks need
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. moveIntent's square-denial branch names ONE of their engine-preferred moves that the played move now covers (moveIntent.ts:464-487); moveFundamentals' prophylaxis covers only a pawn push denying an enemy minor a square (moveFundamentals.ts:732-737). Nothing names 'their rooks can no longer use these squares' as a lasting asset of the piece.

teachingMoves.move: A self-block you control: a pawn put on your bishop's colour restricts it for now, but it holds squares the bishop cannot reach and a capture can reopen the diagonal whenever you choose, so it is no real concession
teachingMoves.example: Pushing to d5 seems to bury your b7-bishop, and for the moment it does. But the pawn controls e4, the bishop will protect a pawn that later recaptures on e4, and you can reopen the diagonal any time by taking on c4. No hurry: finish developing first.
teachingMoves.when: Committal central pawn moves onto your own bishop's colour
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. bishopBlockingPawns names the pawn in the bishop's way (positionReadingService.ts:484); the bad-bishop note ignores a bishop still at home (positionReadingService.ts:546-547); theirMoveCost's bishop-shut kind reports only the cost (theirMoveCost.ts:94-115). Nothing reads that a capture is available to reopen the line, or that the blocking pawn is guarded by that bishop.

teachingMoves.move: Judge the opponent's pawn break by its answer: if the pawn it hits can simply advance past it, the break is not a threat yet
teachingMoves.example: Their ...c5 break doesn't worry you: if it comes, d5 runs past it and gains space.
teachingMoves.when: The opponent prepares a pawn break against your centre
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (5703); sharpens an earlier reader's 'an idea is not a threat'
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: PARTIAL. falseAlarm needs a concrete threat from detectNewThreat (falseAlarm.ts:37, :52-53; kinds mate / fork / capture at groundedAnswer.ts:6865), so a quiet pawn break never reaches it; moveIntent reads only a move already played (moveIntent.ts:124).

teachingMoves.move: Count the enemy king's flight squares: a king with none means the next check may be mate, so bring the heavy pieces in
teachingMoves.example: After the h-file trades their king steps to f7 and has no square left at all; that is the signal to bring your queen in.
teachingMoves.when: Kingside attacks after the shelter has been broken
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (5944); about 3 across the corpus (4679, 5289, 5944)
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING as a standing read. kingSafetyRead counts shield pawns and open files, not flight squares (positionReadingService.ts:1760); kingAttack's kinds are strips-shelter / removes-defender / adds-attacker / heads-for-king / opens-lines / opens-file (kingAttack.ts:26); moveInsight.escapeSquareFirst counts the king's squares only for one check the engine is about to give (moveInsight.ts:701, :716); the king-safety concept text tells the student to count flight squares (conceptEngine.ts:782) but no computer does.

teachingMoves.move: Post-mortem on a piece: name the piece that did nothing all game and why its planned road was a dead end
teachingMoves.example: Looking back, their knight on a6 never did anything: its only road ran through c5, and their own pawn ended up standing there.
teachingMoves.when: When the game is decided, looking back over the opponent's plan
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. thinkAloud.opponentHabits counts only minors still at home and repeated moves (thinkAloud.ts:180); pieceScope and strongestWeakestPiece read one position (positionReadingService.ts:787, :1140). A per-game history of each piece's scope would answer 'idle all game'.

teachingMoves.move: Name the small pawn formation a set-up builds and what it is for
teachingMoves.example: a6 together with b5 and c6 makes a small pawn triangle that backs the queenside expansion; the same triangle in other set-ups gives the dark bishop a safe home on d6.
teachingMoves.when: Set-up building moves in the opening
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 in slice (5767); about 3 across the corpus (544, 5198, 5767)
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING. namedPawnStructure knows the French chain, the closed centre, the isolated queen's pawn and hanging pawns only (positionReadingService.ts:1060-1134).

summary:
I re-read every note in voiced-teachings notes 5702-6145 (444 notes, 27 videos). Before keeping any act I searched the full 12-reader digest (docs/plans/swarm-inputs/digests/teach.md) for it by keyword. The two coarse readers whose ranges cover this slice already caught most of what it does: outposts and routes, recapture choice, trading on your own terms, keeping the queens on against a stuck king, kicking the central knight, checks from a distance, in-between moves, ignoring the slower wing, not h4 before they castle.

I am returning 24 entries: 20 acts that are not in the digest, and 4 sharpenings of acts it already has, each with a new code finding (structural threat, the in-between move's record half, the development bind, a break that isn't a threat).

Highest value for the opening (F02):
- a piece in front of its own pawn turns a neighbouring pawn into an isolated pawn in all but name (5748);
- a resource that bites only after their commitment, such as the check on b4 saved until their knight is on c3 (5905);
- a capture that is sound only with one specific follow-up (6035);
- a pawn grab refuted because the queen trade costs your king castling (6039);
- preparing a recapture with a piece so a pin can't damage your pawns (6023);
- the king hiding behind the attacker's own bishop in the Bxf7 attack, and the forcing move that clears it (6045-6046).

CODE FINDINGS (read-only). Line numbers are against HEAD f00cf6a. Another session has uncommitted edits in the worktree: positionReadingService.ts (+18 lines after line 258) and CoachTeachPage.tsx.

1. F4/F5, a computer that teaches but never records.
- The in-between move is taught (thinkAloud.ts:145, called at :273; moveInsight.ts:642, called only from PuzzleBoard.tsx:652).
- It is never posed: positionPosed's comment says it covers the autopilot recapture (moveInsight.ts:731-732), but its body does not (:743-761).
- It is never classified: 'zwischenzug', 'deflection' and 'interference' are TacticType members (types/index.ts:1714, 1709, 1713) with no live detector (tacticVocabulary.ts:58-64). A miss in a real game is filed under another motif or 'tactical_sequence' (missedTacticService.ts:770-808).
- Result: from games, the heat map can never turn these red or green.

2. V14, a cap that changes other computers' answers.
- findPieceQuality sorts good notes first and keeps four (positionReadingService.ts:604-605).

Close second reading of public/data/voiced-teachings.json notes[6146..6589]: 444 notes from 30 videos, every note read (dumped by index and replayed with chess.js). 61 teaching acts catalogued below, each mapped to a computer in src/services with file:line, or marked MISSING / PARTIAL.

HEADLINE. Many of the reference coach's habits already have a computer, built since the speed-run study:
- speedRunReads.ts: 27 reads
- thinkAloud.ts: lineAchieves, sayLine, notYet, obviousStopFlaw
- deliberation, moveIntent, opponentIntent, bluffDetector, falseAlarm, refutedAlternativeCore, conversionMethod, stalemateWatch, tempoCount, ruleException, theirMoveCost, openingIdentity, theirOpeningVerdict

What this slice adds is the finer layer the coarse readers missed. Eight clusters:
1. POSITIONAL reasons for rejecting a candidate. Deliberation only rules a move out for dropping material, being clearly worse or less precise, or trading queens (deliberation.ts:66). It never rejects for cutting a defensive contact, giving up the bishop pair, blocking a future rook file, or conceding a square.
2. Pin nuances. A pin can ban a capture while still allowing a push. The pinned piece stops counting as a defender. Pins can be compared, kept through a recapture, or made permanent once the bishop that could challenge the pinner is gone.
3. The IMMUNE piece: it can be taken, but taking it walks into a fork.
4. Restricting an ENEMY piece with your own pawn.
5. Trade geometry: which side's file the trade opens, keep pieces on when you have more space, trade to defuse an attack, and trade only when the trade comes free.
6. The goal → obstacle → remove-it chain (F0c, not built).
7. About eight missing habits, for example: start calculating with the simplest move; when a file opens toward the kings, look for checks on the second or seventh rank; before grabbing with the queen, list her escapes; look for an in-between move before moving an attacked queen.
8. Line familiarity in Learn ('you've met this many times', 'you haven't faced the main line'). This exists only as a Review intro, which still speaks numbers.

FOUND IN PASSING, verified by running the real detectors from the scratchpad (read-only):

(a) D10 RISK, at the note-6543 board.
- Board: r4rk1/pp3pb1/2npp2p/2q1n1p1/4P2P/1B2NbB1/P1PQNPP1/1R3RK1 w
- The reference coach teaches that Black's bishop on f3 is immune: gxf3 Nxf3+ forks king and queen.
- findHangingBySee (positionReadingService.ts:361) returns that bishop as hanging, gain 2.
- findRemovableGuards (tacticsDetector.ts:629) offers White 'the knight on e5 is the only defender of the bishop on f3 — and it can be taken'. But Bxe5 is answered by Nxe5, which restores the guard.
- heldByTactic (speedRunReads.ts:162) cannot catch it. It requires more attackers than defenders (:169) and gives up whenever SEE says the capture wins (:170).

(b) PIN-PRESSURE BLIND SPOT, at the note-6318 board.
- Board: r1bqr1k1/pppn1pbp/3p1np1/8/3BP3/PP1B1N2/2PN1PPP/R2QK2R b KQ
- findPinPressure (pinPressure.ts:85) returns nothing for Black before …d5. canLeaveLine (pinGeometry.ts:80) only counts a pawn's capture when there is already something on the capture square.
- So the pawn strike that creates the bite is exactly the move it can never suggest. After …d5, detectTactics does report the pin.

(c) V8 (numbers in speech).

rhythm:
Measured on the 444 distilled notes (word count of the note text):
- Overall median: 22 words.
- Opening: the student's own moves median 25, the opponent's 18.
- Middlegame: own 24, theirs 21.
- Endgame: own 19, theirs 11.

17% of notes are a bare move statement of 8 words or fewer. That rises to 28% on the opponent's middlegame moves and 36% on the opponent's endgame moves. Recaptures, king shuffles and forced replies get one clause, never a lecture.

Long notes (60+ words, 15 in all) come at decisions and lean early:
- 9 are tagged opening, and all 15 fall by ply 34. This matches F02 (opening first).
- Examples: a three-candidate recapture decision (#6309, 317 words); the plan for a whole gambit main line (#6241, 411 words); a gambit's idea (#6306, 115); a strategic defence plus a habit (#6279); a calculated rejection of a candidate (#6526, 95); the queen-escape check (#6525); a calculation habit (#6442); a game's whole-board lessons (#6313, 177).

Order inside a long note is stable:
1. Frame the moment as a decision.
2. List the candidates.
3. Give each one's consequence.
4. The geometric check that settles it (escape squares, who guards what).
5. The line with their best reply.
6. Their likely mistake and why.
7. A safety check before cashing in.
8. The simplest win.
9. A closing maxim or habit.

Other patterns:
- In two book runs (#6226-6237, #6242-6252), one thought spans several plies while the moves go quickly: the narration is about the line, not the ply.
- 127 of 414 consecutive-note transitions skip at least one ply, so the distilled corpus does not carry a note on every ply.
- Opponent moves are framed by INTENT ('they are steering into X', 'that is a mediocre choice') rather than described.
- About 12 notes pose a rhetorical question and answer it at once.
- About 20 notes speak in the first person ('I like', 'I got greedy'). The act inside them, usually a better alternative, is kept; the self-reference must go (V1).

summary:
I read all 444 notes in the slice (6590–7033): 19 videos, split 176 opening, 169 middlegame and 99 endgame. They contain 63 distinct teaching acts. I checked each one against the teaching census (2026-09-27) and the insight catalogue in docs/. 35 are new or only partly covered. Of those 35, 20 have no computer at all and 15 are partial: a computer reaches the fact but cannot say the mechanism, or it is wired for one seat only.

One finding about the brief comes first. Its FIRST GEM does not work as written. The line is 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6 3.Bc4 Bg4 4.Bxf7+ Kxf7 5.Ng5+. After 5.Ng5+, chess.js lists 5...Qxg5 among Black's legal replies: the d8 queen sees g5 through the empty e7 and f6 squares. After 5...Qxg5 the g4 bishop is guarded by the queen, so White is simply down a piece. Even the line as written (5...Ke8 6.Qxg4) only nets one pawn: material comes out 36 to 35.

Note 6601 is the real-game version where the pattern does work. It is an Alapin position after 7...Qxd6 8.O-O, and the coach calls ...Bg4 there "an incredibly common blunder". On that board no Black piece attacks g5 and nothing guards g4 (the Black queen is on d6), so 9.Bxf7+ Kxf7 10.Ng5+ followed by 11.Qxg4 is legal. By count it still nets only a pawn plus Black's castling rights; I could not get an engine value (no binary at /usr/games/stockfish). Under F04 this is a pattern taught with its conditions, not a trap. Note 6601 is the right position to teach it on, and the brief's line is the right position to show it failing. None of the 344 gems in src/data/punish-gems.json contains Bxf7+ followed by Ng5+, and none holds the Fried Liver slip (recapturing with the knight on d5) that note 6801 warns against.

The most valuable missed acts, opening first per F02:
- A pattern taught by the condition that decides it.
- En passant as a structural weapon.
- Which move commits you to an opening, and which moves are only gateways.
- An opening rule of thumb stated with its reason.
- A purposeless opponent move treated as a free tempo whose cost arrives later.
- Choosing h3 over f3 by what each weakens.
- The Greek-gift conditions used defensively ("castle, it doesn't work here"). This is an F4 gap: moveInsight.greekGift (moveInsight.ts:668) only fires when the sacrifice is the best move.
- Their own piece blocking their own pawn or development.
- Don't kick a misplaced enemy piece; the attack only improves it.
- The principle of two weaknesses.
- Self-interference: the checking piece blocks your own line to the flight square.
- A mating net one guard away, with the trap that needs one natural pawn push.
- Trapping a piece, or fixing a king in place, by taking its last escape square first. escapeSquareFirst (moveInsight.ts:701) covers only a check that becomes mate.
- The castling rule when it is the obstacle.
- Counting the pawn-storm race; planRace (planRace.ts:180) deliberately excludes it.
- Imbalance trading rules for two minors against a rook.
- Engine verdict versus practical difficulty. The census calls this "not a computer", but scanCriticality (criticalityScan.ts:103) run for both sides would compute it.

Defects in the shipped corpus (public/data/voiced-teachings.json; S7 speaks these in "teach me X opening"), all checked on the board:
- Note 6720 says a8=N is checkmate; the stored position is not even check.
- Note 6984 says the rook underpromotion avoids stalemate, but e8=Q+ also gives check with the same four king replies.
- Note 6984 says Re5 starts a mate in two; after either king reply (Kc3 or Kc4) White has no mate in one.
- Notes 6733–6737 are tagged studentSide black but tell the student White's moves ("you don't play a knight to f3"), a V16 seat inversion.
- In notes 6834–6835 the student is White, but White's own 2.Ba6 is narrated as the opponent's move and Black's recapture as the student's.
- "elephant", a transcription error for "Alapin", appears 8 times corpus-wide, 4 in this slice (6592, 6614, 6721, 6722).
- Note 6995 says "Panov" where the King's Indian line is the Panno, and attributes a recommendation to a named player (F0d).
- Garbled text at 6996 ("onethe") and 6999 ("Heretwo").
- 42 of 444 notes speak in the first person (V1), and 3 cite ratings (V8).

Two items in the catalogue need care:
- Its "Imbalances" bullet (line 408) says two minors against a rook usually favour the rook. This slice teaches the opposite (6637, 6887, 6892).
- Its type 12 copies "activity matters less in an endgame" (from 6927). That is unsound as a general rule; build only the defensible form: without queens, their active pieces cannot build a mating attack.
rhythm:
Measured on this slice. The corpus is a compressed paraphrase; the thinkAloud.ts header measured the raw spoken narration at about 50 words a move (20–47 on routine moves, 90–133 at decisions), so these counts understate the spoken length.

- Opening: 176 notes, median 18 words, mean 22.5. 34 notes are 8 words or fewer and 25 are 40 or more (longest 143).
- Middlegame: 169 notes, median 19, mean 25.5. 29 are 8 words or fewer and 29 are 40 or more (longest 146).
- Endgame: 99 notes, median 12, mean 12.4. 35 are 8 words or fewer and none reach 40 (longest 35).
- 60 of 444 notes are bare restatements of the move ("Black recaptures on d5."), always on routine replies.
- 192 of 444 notes sit on the opponent's move: he narrates their moves too, usually as what it wants, what it cost them, or what they should have played.

Shape:
- In the opening, a lecture video (the Alapin, notes 6590–6618) gives every move several points: theory status, the move's job, what the opponent could have played and why that is scary, and the plan ahead. Speed-run games give routine book moves one clause and spend words where the opponent deviates (6629: their a3 is a wasted move).
- Long notes cluster at decision points (6604, 6617, 6618, 6802). Their internal order: the move's real point, then what it fixes or denies, then the tempting alternative and why it helps the opponent, then the line with their reply, then a list of things to watch, then one general lesson ("two weaknesses", "calculate on your turn").
- The middlegame alternates one-clause moves with a full weighing whenever there are real candidates (6611 changes its mind twice).
- The endgame is one technical clause per move ("king first", "push, don't grab") plus a safety check before the finish (stalemate, 6705–6719). The game closes on a one-sentence moral (6720, 6758).
- Foreshadowing ("there's a concrete point coming", "I'm anticipating b6") and rhetorical questions answered at once ("Where does the knight go?") carry the thread from move to move.

teachingMoves.move: [NEW] Teach a trap pattern by the condition that decides it, on a real position where the condition holds
teachingMoves.example: Note 6601 names ...Bg4 as a very common blunder after the queen recaptures on d6 in this Alapin, but gives no refutation. On the board the refutation is the rulebook's own pattern: the bishop takes f7 with check, the knight jumps out of the pin with check, and the queen takes g4. It works here because their queen on d6 cannot reach g5 and nothing guards g4 (chess.js: no Black attacker of either square). In the brief's own first-gem line it fails, because the queen on d8 simply takes the knight on g5.
teachingMoves.when: Opening, before the opponent's most natural mistake
teachingMoves.frequency: 1 note (6601). Neither the census nor the catalogue frames it as a condition check.
teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING: there is no 'pin broken with check' computer (questions.md item 7). 0 of 344 gems in src/data/punish-gems.json contain 'Bxf7+ ... Ng5+', so the Learn gem lane (computerRoles.ts:47 → punishGems) has nothing to voice.

teachingMoves.move: [NEW] En passant as a structural weapon, and as a decision
teachingMoves.example: 6597: the reply they didn't play was the scary ...c4, because once you push d4 they take en passant and break your chain, leaving e5 without its base. 6598: take en passant now, or they get their ideal setup with the bishop out to g4; taking also keeps your bishop's diagonal open.

teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: MISSING: no teaching computer mentions en passant (it appears only in edge-case handling in pinGeometry.ts, positionFacts.ts and groundedAnswer.ts).

teachingMoves.move: [NEW] Name the move that commits you to an opening, and the moves that only open doors
teachingMoves.example: 6991: you haven't chosen the King's Indian yet; d6 commits you, while c6 and d5 could still head for a Grünfeld-style setup. 7008: their c3 has no value of its own, it's a doorway to the London, the Torre or a fianchetto, so wait for them to show their cards.

Computable from openings-lichess.json by comparing the set of named lines reachable before and after the move.

teachingMoves.move: [NEW] State an opening's rule of thumb together with the reason that makes it true
teachingMoves.example: 6629-6630: the central break is almost playable, but before you castle their bishop check on b5 pins your c6 knight against your king. So in this opening the rule is: break in the centre only after castling.

teachingMoves.example: 6629: their a3 stops nothing, because nothing of yours was heading for b4, so play as if you'd been handed a free move. 6636, moves later: they pay for that a3 now, because in the normal version their king would already be castled. 6806 notes the same kind of move in another game.

teachingMoves.example: 6743: to keep their knight off g4 you can push the rook pawn or the bishop pawn. Nearly always take the rook pawn, because the bishop pawn weakens far too much, and with your king going long the h-pawn also becomes the anchor for a later push at their king.

teachingMoves.computerThatCouldProduceIt: Partial: moveInsight.emptyThreat (moveInsight.ts:909) catches 'the target steps away and you are no better', not 'the target ends up better'. Needs piece quality (pieceValueRead) compared before and after the retreat.
